pull.title: util: cap Sock::WaitMany timeout to fix -rpcclienttimeout=0 on macOS
pull.body:
`bitcoin-cli -rpcclienttimeout=0` is documented as "no timeout", but on macOS it fails with "Could not connect to the server" since #34342 (it's in v32.0rc1/rc2).

bitcoin-cli turns 0 into `std::chrono::years(5)` and passes it to `Sock::Wait`. On platforms without `USE_POLL` (everything except Linux) `WaitMany` uses `select()`, and macOS returns EINVAL for timeouts above 10^8 seconds. Five years is about 1.58 * 10^8 s. The same happens with any explicit value above 10^8, e.g. `-rpcclienttimeout=110000000`. On Linux, `poll()` takes the timeout as an int, so the millisecond count gets narrowed. For five years this happens to wrap to a negative value, which means infinite, so it works there by accident.

This caps the timeout in `Sock::WaitMany` at INT_MAX milliseconds (about 24.8 days). That fits `poll()` and is below the 31 days POSIX requires `select()` to support. Doing it in `WaitMany` covers every caller, not only bitcoin-cli.

The new `sock_tests/wait_large_timeout` test waits with a 5 year timeout on a socket that already has data. It fails on master on macOS and passes with this change. I also checked by hand on macOS that `-rpcclienttimeout=0`, `157784760` and `2147483647` work against a running node, and `interface_bitcoin_cli.py` still passes.

This doesn't overlap with #36299, which changes how the timeout is counted but still passes the 5 year value down.

concept ACK

---
could we handle the "_no timeout_" case using the OS primitives' native
indefinite timeout, while keeping this cap for explicitly specified large
finite timeouts ?

since `poll()` supports a negative timeout and `select()` can take `NULL`, that
would preserve the `-rpcclienttimeout=0` semantics without removing the
protection against very large finite values

references:

- Linux [`poll(2)`](https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/poll.2.html)
- FreeBSD [`select(2)`](https://man.freebsd.org/cgi/man.cgi?query=select&sektion=2)
- OpenBSD [`select(2)`](https://man.openbsd.org/select.2)
- NetBSD [`select(2)`](https://man.netbsd.org/select.2)
- Windows [`select()`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/api/winsock2/nf-winsock2-select)

> [!NOTE]
>  i do not have an Apple machine to check the macOS local manpages. so macOS users
can just check the authoritative local versions with `man 2 select` and `man 2
poll`

thanks! good call, pushed a second commit that does this.

you're right that the cap alone isn't really "no timeout". `HTTPClient::Recv` treats any wait that comes back empty as a timeout, so `-rpcclienttimeout=0` would have given up after ~24.8 days of silence. I doubt anyone is going to keep a `waitfornewblock` open for three and a half weeks, but "no timeout" should probably mean no timeout.

fwiw the 5 years was never really "no timeout" either. it's a leftover from libevent, which just couldn't wait indefinitely (b3b26e149c).

I do have a Mac on my desk, so here's what the man pages say: `select(2)` "blocks indefinitely" with a NULL timeout and returns EINVAL if the timeout is "negative or too large". `poll(2)` blocks indefinitely with -1. same as the BSDs.

what the new commit does:
- adds `Sock::NO_TIMEOUT` (`milliseconds::max()`), which `WaitMany` passes as `-1` to `poll()` and `nullptr` to `select()`
- bitcoin-cli uses it for `-rpcclienttimeout=0` instead of 5 years
- the cap from the first commit stays for large finite values like `-rpcclienttimeout=110000000`

added `sock_tests/wait_no_timeout`. I also checked by hand on macOS that `-rpcclienttimeout=0 waitfornewblock` waits until a block comes in, and that `-rpcclienttimeout=1` still times out.

this will conflict with #36299 since both touch the deadline code in cli. whichever goes in second gets a small rebase.

I wonder how much we want to backport here. I doubt there is a use case to have a timeout of more than a few hours, so capping to 1 day, or even 14 days, or the first commit should be fine for a backport?

> capping to 1 day

I agree. The second commit might've gone overboard

makes sense, dropped the second commit so this is just the cap in `Sock::WaitMany` and should be easy to backport. that fixes both `-rpcclienttimeout=0` and large explicit values; 0 now effectively means ~24.8 days, which as you say is way beyond any real use.

@winterrdog the native infinite wait (poll -1 / select NULL) can go in a follow-up if people still want it.

> the native infinite wait (poll -1 / select NULL) can go in a follow-up if people still want it.

A protracted wait timeout is simple and does the job fine. So, no need to get dogmatic about native infinite wait 

Approach ACK

util: cap Sock::WaitMany timeout

bitcoin-cli turns -rpcclienttimeout=0 into a 5 year timeout and passes
it down to Sock::Wait. On systems without poll() (e.g. macOS and the
BSDs) the wait is done with select(), which fails with EINVAL for
timeouts above 10^8 seconds on macOS. So since the libevent removal in
#34342, `bitcoin-cli -rpcclienttimeout=0 ...` fails on macOS with
"Could not connect to the server". With poll(), the millisecond count
is narrowed to int, so large values can wrap as well.

Cap the timeout at INT_MAX milliseconds (about 24.8 days), which fits
poll() and stays below the 31 days that POSIX requires select() to
accept.

events.body: @winterrdog thanks, took both. The comment is shortened as you suggested, and the test now starts `Wait()` in a thread with the 5 year timeout and only sends the data after 100ms, so `select()`/`poll()` really wait with it. Without the cap it still fails on macOS (the wait returns false right away), with the cap it passes. Kept it as a single commit for the backport.

from: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36340#issuecomment-5847188854

> I doubt anyone is going to keep a `waitfornewblock` open for three and a half weeks, but "no timeout" should probably mean no timeout.



from: https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/pull/36340#issuecomment-5865455142

> I doubt there is a use case to have a timeout of more than a few hours, so capping to 1 day, or even 14 days

---

those 2 comments got me thinking.. about this:


https://github.com/bitcoin/bitcoin/blob/dc2a9987aab711abdc1a77aa6d1462c6a46deabd/src/bitcoin-cli.cpp#L1205-L1206

why don't we use sth much shorter than 5 years? even 1-4 days feels like plenty of room here

i mean.. contemporary humans are known to get frustrated when a webpage takes more than [7-10 seconds](https://arxiv.org/html/2101.09086v1#abstract1) to load. if someone is still waiting for an RPC response after 6 hours (or even 30 minutes), they have probably entered a new dimension of patience

i think this could be a follow-up if we do not want to make the PR's diff bigger. just throwing the idea out there. 

what do you think ?

agree 5 years doesn't mean much in practice, and with the cap it's already ~24.8 days at most anyway. I'd rather keep this PR as is so it stays a small backport though. Changing what 0 means would also need the help text updated, since it currently says "0 for no timeout", so it seems like its own discussion. Happy to open a follow-up for it after this one, or review yours if you want to take it.

> Happy to open a follow-up for it after this one, 

Sure. That's fine

> > Happy to open a follow-up for it after this one,
> 
> Sure. That's fine

thanks. I'll open it once this one is merged. there's no code conflict between the two (this PR only touches `Sock::WaitMany`, the follow-up would change the 5 year value in `bitcoin-cli.cpp` and the help text), it's more about keeping them apart: this one is tagged for 32.x backport and only fixes the bug, while shortening what 0 means is a behaviour change that shouldn't be backported. if both were open at the same time the "what should 0 mean" discussion would probably end up here too. I'll also check it against #36299 since that touches the same cli timeout code.

intentional ?

few bytes, so that we actually make `select()`/`poll()` wait with the large timeout.
sth like starting `Wait()` in a separate thread, waiting briefly (say `50` or
`100` ms), then sending the data from the main thread. that way we exercise the
full `Wait()` path with the large timeout passed and make sure it completes
without a hitch, rather than just checking that `Wait()` accepts it

or is the current test enough to cover the regression ?
